report:
**Conclusion:** Your claim is supported, most directly for *chlorhexidine–alcohol versus iodine–alcohol* skin preparation before cesarean delivery.

The pivotal randomized trial (1,147 women, single center) found surgical-site infection in 4.0% with chlorhexidine–alcohol versus 7.3% with iodine–alcohol (relative risk 0.55, 95% CI 0.34–0.90; P=0.02). That is an absolute reduction of 3.3 percentage points (about 1 fewer infection per 30 preparations). Adverse skin reactions were similar.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048

A cesarean-specific systematic review/meta-analysis of randomized trials also concluded chlorhexidine–alcohol reduces SSI compared with povidone–iodine preparations. A 2020 Cochrane review judged the evidence **moderate certainty**, characterizing chlorhexidine as probably *slightly* more effective than povidone–iodine overall.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184558/  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32580252/

**Important qualification:** Results are not uniformly statistically significant in every comparison. The CAPICA randomized trial found no significant difference (about 6.3% vs 7.0%), but compared chlorhexidine–alcohol with an **aqueous** povidone–iodine scrub-and-paint protocol—not iodine–alcohol. Thus it weakens any claim of a large universal advantage, but does not directly contradict the specific iodine–alcohol finding.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28599898/

Overall, chlorhexidine–alcohol is a reasonable evidence-based preferred option when no contraindication exists, while the expected benefit is modest in absolute terms and local protocols, allergy, alcohol safety/drying time, and product availability matter.
